catalog_locator: Sec. 1.4.1 'Stress and the Phonological Word', subsections 'Phonetic Realisation of Stress' and 'Interaction between Stress and Tone', article pp. 13-14 (= PDF pp. 24-25; page images opsl1_pages/; scanned); endnote 6, article p. 31 (= PDF p. 42); 'Stress Perturbation' pp. 15-17; sec. 1.3 'Tone' pp. 7-13; sec. 1.5.1 'The Phonological Phrase'.
catalog_quote: The phonological word (PW) is the domain of single stress contour. Every PW has a stress pattern with one and only one primary stress, plus optional secondary stress if the PW has more than two syllables. ... Stress is realised by the following phonetic features: (1) Greater force (2) Greater length (3) Greater contrast in vowel quality (4) Greater contrast between the tones ... As a result it can be difficult to hear which syllable of a two-syllable word is stressed, but in a four-syllable word it is very clear. ... Interaction between Stress and Tone Stress placement in Mündü is primarily a function of high pitch and position in the PW, such that: (1) Any word with only one high tone syllable will place stress on that syllable. ... (2) Any word with all high-tone syllables will place primary stress on the first syllable, with secondary stress on the last syllable if it is a word of more than two syllables. ... (3) Any word with non-adjacent high-tone syllables will place primary stress on the last high-tone syllable and secondary stress on the first high-tone syllable. ... (4) In all other words primary stress is placed on the penultimate syllable and there is no secondary stress.
world_status: statement found in an open source

The quoted passage is on pp.13-14 exactly as reported: sec. 1.4.1 'Stress and the Phonological Word' opens 'The phonological word (PW) is the domain of single stress contour. Every PW has a stress pattern with one and only one primary stress, plus optional secondary stress if the PW has more than two syllables.'; the subsection 'Interaction between Stress and Tone' (p.14) reads 'Stress placement in Mundu [M-u-umlaut-nd-u-umlaut] is primarily a function of high pitch and position in the PW, such that: (1) Any word with only one high tone syllable will place stre…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mündü has three level lexical/grammatical tones (H, M, L) and, in addition, one primary stress per phonological word whose position is predictable from the tone pattern: stress goes to the sole H-toned syllable if there is exactly one; in all-H words to the first syllable; with non-adjacent H's to the last H; and in every other word (no H, or adjacent H's with other tones) to the penultimate syllable. Stress is realised as greater force, length, vowel-quality contrast and exaggerated tone contrast, and is hard to perceive in disyllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Optional secondary stress only in words of three or more syllables: on the last syllable of all-H words, on the first H of words with non-adjacent H's; none under the default penultimate rule. Realised by the same features as primary stress to a lesser degree.
new_statements.exceptions: Endnote 6 (p. 31): 'A few exceptions to this rule [rule 4, penultimate] have been found:' four nouns glossed 'rain', 'woman' (stress not penultimate) and 'child', 'water gourd' (initial stress). 'Stress Perturbation' (pp. 15-17): certain syntactic frames shift stress, e.g. before the completive particle (e)yi the key word's final syllable acquires H tone and primary stress (sometimes yielding two primary stresses); before ne 'this' all-H words move primary stress to the final syllable and no-H words to the final syllable; in another frame all-L words shift primary stress to the first syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (PW), described as a stress/timing unit (roughly stress-timed rhythm); rules illustrated with nouns in citation-like frames ('ma ceka ___ esikine' etc.). Above the word, the phonological phrase (sec. 1.5.1) has an intonational peak, usually on a PW near the end, whose stressed syllable receives extra force/length/height. The authors note it 'can be difficult to hear which syllable of a two-syllable word is stressed'.
new_statements.identity_note: Jeffrey & Polley 1981 describe Mündü as spoken around Maridi and Yei (Western Equatoria, South Sudan), data recorded in the Maridi area 1978-1980; they state dialect differences between the Sudan and Zaire communities are minimal. Same language as Glottolog mund1326 (Mündü/Mundu/Mondo).

new_statements.quote: 2. Tone and Stress 2a. There appear to be three main tone levels in these languages—High, Mid, and Low. Rising and Falling tones are common outside NDOGO-SERE, but seem for the most part to be the result of assimilation. Tone classes in Nouns and Verbs have been noted; tone also plays a grammatical role in Verb conjugation. [...] 2b. Stress is often responsible for changes in vowel quality and vowel length. In MAYOGO there is a tendency towards vowel length on the penultimate syllable. In NGBAKA, GBAYA, and BANDA, on the other hand, there is a tendency towards extra shortness here. Compare Eboué's BANDA spellings yavro (dog), yabru (goat), akblo (child) with Hackett's TOGBO renderings yavoró, aboro, agbolo. 3. Word Shape

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees on type: a tone language with three level tones (= Jeffrey & Polley 1981's H/M/L) in which stress also operates. Adds nothing on Mündü stress placement: the bibliography's locator 'sec. 2b Stress' points to a group-level paragraph about Mayogo/Ngbaka/Gbaya/Banda vowel length that is silent on Mundu, so it neither confirms nor contradicts Jeffrey & Polley's tone-and-position stress rule. The bib tag 'not read: abstract or record only' can be upgraded to 'snippet-read: sec. 2 reconstructed; silent on Mündü stress placement'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level statement for the Sere-Mundu / Banda-Gbaya-Ngbandi languages (MUNDU is one of the languages tabulated in the chapter): three level tones (High, Mid, Low), lexical and grammatical; the whole 2b 'Stress' paragraph says only that stress often changes vowel quality and length, with penultimate vowel length in MAYOGO and extra shortness in NGBAKA, GBAYA, BANDA. It names no stress position for MUNDU and contains no Mundu-specific stress remark; other 'MUNDU' + 'stress' co-occurrences in the volume (held probes) are the 2b headings of other chapters (Bilin, Moru-Ma'di, Mangbetu) and non-prosodic Mundu mentions (consonants, plural, pronouns).
new_statements.exceptions: none for Mundu; MAYOGO penultimate vowel length vs NGBAKA/GBAYA/BANDA penultimate shortness are the only language-specific remarks in 2b
new_statements.identity_note: Jeffrey & Polley 1981 (catalog source) describe Mündü of southern Sudan (SIL, Juba/Maridi area). Tucker & Bryan 1966's chapter is a group sketch of Sere-Mundu and Banda-Gbaya-Ngbandi built on Santandrea's Ndogo-Sere material, Tucker's own MAYOGO (Niangara) notes and Congo sources; MUNDU appears in its comparative tables (Sudan/Congo Mündü not distinguished in the fragments). Santandrea 1950 treats Mondu = Mündü of the western Bahr-el-Ghazal alongside Indri, Togoyo, Ndogo, Feroge, Mangaya (per title and reviews; unverified against the work).
